questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the lobe handling visual processing
questions.stem: A transit planner notices a driver who cannot recognize faces after a stroke; which lobe was likely damaged?

options.text: Occipital lobe, because it houses primary visual cortex
Parietal lobe, because it maps spatial attention across scenes
options.misconception: attributes face blindness to spatial attention

options.text: Frontal lobe, because it plans motor actions for scanning faces
options.misconception: confuses motor planning with visual recognition

options.text: Temporal lobe, because it stores all long term memories
options.misconception: overstates memory storage as the cause

questions.explanation: Face recognition begins in visual cortex of the occipital lobe, so damage there disrupts seeing faces. Temporal regions refine identity but the core deficit follows occipital injury. The tempting wrong idea blames memory storage instead of perception.
questions.hint: Think about where visual input first lands.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: During a board review, a commuter with left hemisphere damage struggles to speak; what does this show?

options.text: Right hemisphere solely controls all language output
Left hemisphere usually dominates language production
Both hemispheres contribute equally to speech
Language is stored only in the corpus callosum

questions.explanation: In most people language production relies on left hemisphere regions, so left damage impairs speech. Right hemisphere roles are more spatial and prosodic. Equal contribution is not the typical pattern.
questions.hint: Recall the usual side for speech.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the structure for emotional memory
questions.stem: The planning team maps a cyclist with heightened fear responses after amygdala lesion reversal; what structure regulates fear?

options.text: Hippocampus, because it encodes spatial routes
Thalamus, because it relays all sensory input
Amygdala, because it detects threat signals

questions.explanation: The amygdala evaluates threat and triggers fear responses. Hippocampus handles context and memory. Thalamus relays but does not decide emotional salience. Balance is cerebellar.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish short term from long term memory stores
questions.stem: A supervisor flags a passenger who repeats a phone number for seconds then forgets it; which store failed?

options.text: Short term store, because capacity and duration are limited
Long term store, because encoding never happened
options.misconception: assumes long term failure from brief retention

options.text: Sensory store, because input faded too fast
options.misconception: confuses sensory decay with rehearsal failure

options.text: Procedural store, because skill was not formed
options.misconception: mislabels a fact as a skill

questions.explanation: Repeating briefly then forgetting reflects short term memory limits. Long term storage was not attempted. Sensory memory fades in under a second, too brief here.
questions.hint: Duration of holding is the clue.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Link frontal lobe to executive control
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic shows poor planning and impulsivity after frontal injury; explain the executive deficit.

answer.exemplar: Frontal regions govern planning, inhibition, and goal-directed behavior. Damage there weakens executive control, producing impulsivity and poor organization. The mechanic's symptoms fit this pattern rather than a sensory loss.

questions.explanation: Frontal injury disrupts executive functions like planning and inhibition, causing impulsivity. It is not a sensory or memory store deficit. Recovery varies with lesion size and rehab.
questions.hint: Executive control lives in the frontal lobe.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Connect sleep loss to cognitive decline
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider with two nights of sleep deprivation and slower reaction times; what is most likely?

options.text: No change because naps compensate fully

questions.explanation: Sleep debt impairs attention and reaction time. Stress hormones may feel alert but do not restore processing speed. Naps help only partly.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define interaction of genes and environment
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler whose anxiety rises only in high stress jobs; what pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Anxiety emerging under stress shows genes and environment interacting. Neither alone explains it. Randomness is not the best account.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Map parietal lobe to touch and space
questions.stem: The safety officer examines a pedestrian with lost touch and spatial sense; which lobe is affected?

options.text: Parietal lobe, because it integrates touch and space
Occipital lobe, because it sees objects
Frontal lobe, because it initiates movement
Temporal lobe, because it hears sounds

questions.explanation: The parietal lobe processes touch and spatial relations. Frontal initiates movement but not sensation. Occipital and temporal handle vision and hearing.
questions.hint: Touch and space share a lobe.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A coordinator tracks a cyclist with right hemisphere damage who cannot navigate maps; what strength was lost?
questions.explanation: The right hemisphere supports spatial navigation and holistic processing. Language and speech are more left lateralized. Arithmetic facts are not the main deficit.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver with anterograde amnesia after hippocampal damage; what is impaired?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is critical for forming new declarative memories. Temperature and hormones are hypothalamic. Eye movements are brainstem and cerebellar.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A transit planner notices synaptic strengthening after repeated stimulation; explain LTP.

answer.exemplar: Long term potentiation strengthens synapses when neurons fire together repeatedly. It supports learning and memory by increasing signal efficiency. The planner's observation matches this cellular mechanism.

questions.explanation: LTP is activity-dependent synaptic strengthening linked to learning. It is not just more neurotransmitter release alone. Repeated co-activation drives it.
questions.hint: Neurons that fire together wire together.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: During a board review, a commuter with Parkinsonian tremor has low dopamine; which function suffers?
questions.explanation: Dopamine supports motor control and reward. Low dopamine produces movement deficits. Vision, hearing, and pain are handled by other systems.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The planning team maps a cyclist who shows extra REM after sleep loss; what is this called?

options.misconception: confuses stage two features with REM

questions.explanation: REM rebound is increased REM after deprivation. Sleep inertia is morning grogginess. Spindles mark stage two. Delta rebound is slow wave recovery.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A supervisor flags a passenger comparing identical and fraternal twins; what can be inferred?

options.text: Greater identical twin similarity suggests genetic influence
Only environment matters for all traits
Twins share no environment at all

questions.explanation: Greater similarity in identical twins suggests genetic influence. Fraternal twins share about half their genes. Environment is shared too.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic cannot process speech sounds after temporal lesion; which function is lost?
questions.explanation: The temporal lobe contains auditory cortex for speech sounds. Motor, somatosensation, and color are handled elsewhere.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider whose corpus callosum is cut and left hand obeys unseen commands; what does this show?

options.text: Language is bilateral in all adults

questions.explanation: Split brain patients show independent hemispheric processing. The left hand is controlled by the right hemisphere, which may not share verbal awareness. Information sharing is disrupted.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler with disrupted hunger and temperature; which structure is key?

options.text: Occipital lobe, because it processes vision
Parietal lobe, because it senses touch

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus regulates hunger, temperature, and other homeostatic drives. Cerebellum, occipital, and parietal do not control drives.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver who rides a bike but cannot recall learning it; what memory type remains?
questions.explanation: Riding a bike without recalling learning reflects implicit procedural memory. Explicit episodic memory would allow conscious recollection. Sensory and working memory are too brief.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A transit planner notices low serotonin linked to mood and sleep; explain its role.

answer.exemplar: Serotonin modulates mood, sleep, and appetite. Low levels are associated with depression and sleep disruption. It is not the only factor, but it contributes to emotional stability.

questions.explanation: Serotonin influences mood and sleep regulation. Low serotonin correlates with depression. It is one of several neurotransmitters involved.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: During a board review, a commuter asks which stage aids physical restoration; what is the answer?
questions.explanation: Slow wave sleep supports physical restoration and growth hormone release. Light sleep and REM serve other roles. Wakeful rest is not a sleep stage.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The planning team maps a cyclist whose gene expression changes with stress; what concept applies?

options.text: Epigenetics, modifying expression without sequence change

questions.explanation: Epigenetics changes gene expression without altering DNA sequence. It is not mutation, selection, or drift. Stress can trigger such changes.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A safety officer examines a pedestrian with weak voluntary movement; which cortical area is likely?

options.text: Primary motor cortex in frontal lobe
Primary visual cortex in occipital lobe

questions.explanation: Primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe initiates voluntary movement. Visual, auditory, and sensory areas do not drive movement.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A coordinator tracks a cyclist with left hemisphere damage who struggles with language and detail; what style was lost?
questions.explanation: The left hemisphere tends toward analytic sequential processing and language. Holistic and prosodic functions are more right lateralized.
questions.hint: Left side likes details and words.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver showing conditioned fear to a tone; which structure is essential?
questions.explanation: The amygdala is essential for fear conditioning. Hippocampus adds context. Cerebellum and brainstem support other functions.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic learns a route and sleeps; explain memory consolidation.

answer.exemplar: Sleep supports consolidation, stabilizing new memories into long term storage. Hippocampal replay during sleep strengthens connections. The mechanic's route memory benefits from this process.

questions.explanation: Consolidation stabilizes memories during sleep. It is not just rest. Replay strengthens neural connections.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider with excessive neural excitation; which neurotransmitter is likely low?
questions.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter; low GABA reduces inhibition. Glutamate is excitatory. Dopamine and serotonin serve other roles.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler with disrupted daily rhythms; which brain region sets the clock?

options.text: Hippocampus, for time of day memory

questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus regulates circadian rhythms. Cerebellum, hippocampus, and amygdala do not set the daily clock.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver reading that heritability of height is 0.8; what does that mean?

options.text: Eighty percent of a person's height is genetic
Environment has no effect on height
Eighty percent of population variance is genetic

questions.explanation: Heritability is a population variance proportion, not individual destiny. Environment still matters. It does not mean height is fixed.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify occipital damage visual field loss
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic with occipital damage reports half the visual field gone; what is this?
questions.explanation: Occipital damage can cause hemianopia, loss of half the visual field. Aphasia is language, apraxia is movement planning, ataxia is coordination.
questions.hint: Half visual field loss has a name.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A transit planner notices both hemispheres cooperate; explain lateralization nuance.

answer.exemplar: Lateralization means one hemisphere is more efficient for a task, not that the other is silent. Both hemispheres collaborate through the corpus callosum. The planner should avoid overclaiming strict separation.

questions.explanation: Lateralization is a bias, not exclusivity. Both sides contribute and communicate. Strict left or right claims are misleading.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: During a board review, a commuter asks which tract carries hippocampal output; what is it?
questions.explanation: The fornix is the main output tract of the hippocampus. Corpus callosum links hemispheres. Optic and pyramidal tracts serve vision and motor.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The planning team maps a cyclist rehearsing a phone number while navigating; which working memory part holds the number?
questions.explanation: The phonological loop holds verbal information like a phone number. Visuospatial sketchpad handles images. Central executive coordinates. Episodic buffer integrates.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A supervisor flags a passenger with Alzheimer's showing low acetylcholine; what function is affected?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine supports memory and attention; its decline is linked to Alzheimer's. Motor, vision, and pain are not its primary roles.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver with rapid eye movements and vivid dreams; which stage is this?
questions.explanation: REM sleep features rapid eye movements and vivid dreams. Stage two has spindles; slow wave is deep. Wakefulness is not sleep.
questions.hint: Rapid eyes plus dreams equals REM.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic compares adopted children to biological and adoptive parents; what is learned?

options.text: Similarity to adoptive parents suggests genes
Similarity to biological parents suggests genes

questions.explanation: Adoption studies compare children to both sets of parents. Similarity to biological parents suggests genetic influence; to adoptive parents suggests environment.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider with nonfluent speech but intact comprehension; which area is damaged?
questions.explanation: Broca's area in the frontal lobe supports speech production; damage yields nonfluent aphasia with preserved comprehension. Wernicke's damage impairs comprehension.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler with fluent but meaningless speech; which area is damaged?

options.text: Wernicke's area in left temporal lobe

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe supports comprehension; damage yields fluent but meaningless speech. Broca's damage is nonfluent.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver asking which structure relays sensory input; what is it?
questions.explanation: The thalamus relays sensory input to cortex. Hypothalamus regulates drives. Hippocampus and amygdala handle memory and emotion.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic forgets an old password after learning a new one; what is this?
questions.explanation: New learning disrupting old memory is retroactive interference. Proactive is old disrupting new. Decay and repression are other accounts.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider with reduced pain after exercise; which chemical is involved?
questions.explanation: Endorphins are natural pain relievers released during exercise. Adrenaline and cortisol are stress hormones. Insulin regulates glucose.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler with poor sleep and frequent illness; explain the link.

answer.exemplar: Sleep supports immune function, so chronic deprivation weakens defenses and raises infection risk. The traveler's illness pattern reflects this. Restoring sleep helps recovery.

questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation impairs immune response. It is not the only cause of illness. Better sleep supports defense.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver whose genes influence the environments they seek; what is this?
questions.explanation: Gene environment correlation occurs when genetic tendencies shape environment exposure. It is not determinism or mutation.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic with insula damage cannot sense internal bodily states; what is lost?
questions.explanation: The insula supports interoception, awareness of internal states. Extroception is external sensing. Proprioception and nociception are specific subtypes.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A transit planner notices a driver with right hemisphere damage speaks flatly; what is impaired?
questions.explanation: The right hemisphere contributes to emotional prosody. Grammar, phonemes, and vocabulary are more left lateralized.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: During a board review, a commuter asks which region monitors conflict and pain; what is it?
questions.explanation: The anterior cingulate cortex monitors conflict and pain. Parietal, motor, and visual areas serve other roles.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The planning team maps a cyclist's recall dropping steeply then leveling; what curve is this?
questions.explanation: The forgetting curve shows rapid initial loss then plateau. Learning curve shows acquisition. Growth and reaction time are different.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A supervisor flags a passenger with low arousal and attention; which neurotransmitter is likely low?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine supports arousal and attention. GABA inhibits. Endorphins relieve pain. Insulin regulates glucose.

questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver with sleep spindles on EEG; which stage is this?
questions.explanation: Sleep spindles mark stage two sleep. REM has eye movements; slow wave is deep; wakefulness is not sleep.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic notes a trait developing similarly across environments; what concept is this?
questions.explanation: Canalization is development buffered to produce similar outcomes across environments. Plasticity is flexibility. Mutation and drift are evolutionary.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider with poor balance and coordination; which structure is implicated?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates balance and movement. Frontal, temporal, and occipital lobes serve other functions.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler better at right ear speech; what does this reflect?
questions.explanation: Right ear advantage for speech reflects left hemisphere language dominance. It is not hearing loss or equal processing.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver asking which limbic area is tied to reward; what is it?
questions.explanation: The septal area is linked to reward and pleasure. Hippocampus handles memory, amygdala fear, thalamus relay.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic remembers words better after semantic than shallow processing; why?
questions.explanation: Deeper semantic processing improves retention. Shallow processing is weaker. Repetition alone is less effective. Memory is not random.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The route analyst studies a rider with disrupted breathing and heart rate; which region is damaged?
questions.explanation: The brainstem regulates breathing and heart rate. Cortex, cerebellum, and limbic system do not control these vitals.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A scheduler observes a traveler with sleep apnea and daytime sleepiness; explain the consequence.

answer.exemplar: Sleep apnea fragments sleep and reduces oxygen, causing daytime sleepiness and cognitive impairment. Treating the airway obstruction restores sleep quality. The traveler's symptoms follow from disrupted sleep.

questions.explanation: Apnea fragments sleep and lowers oxygen, causing daytime sleepiness. Treatment improves sleep. It is not just laziness.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The operations manager reviews a driver reading that genes set limits and environment chooses within them; what concept?
questions.explanation: Range of reaction means genes set limits and environment determines the outcome within them. It is not determinism or mutation.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In the depot, a mechanic with lost touch sensation; which cortical area is affected?
questions.explanation: Somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe processes touch. Motor, auditory, and visual cortices serve other roles.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Note left hemisphere controls right body
questions.stem: A transit planner notices left hemisphere stroke weakens right arm; what principle applies?
questions.explanation: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, called contralateral control. Ipsilateral would be same side.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: During a board review, a commuter asks which structure is central to reward; what is it?
questions.explanation: The nucleus accumbens is central to reward. Hippocampus handles memory, amygdala fear, thalamus relay.
